title: Elisha's Miracles
overview: 2 Kings Chapter 4 highlights a series of powerful miracles performed by the prophet Elisha, demonstrating God's provision, compassion, and power through His servant. The chapter opens with Elisha helping a widow in desperate need, multiplying her oil to pay off debts and save her sons from slavery. It then tells of a Shunammite woman who shows hospitality to Elisha and is blessed with a son, whom Elisha later raises from the dead. The chapter concludes with miracles involving the provision of food during famine and the purification of poisonous stew. These narratives emphasize God's care for the vulnerable, the prophetic authority of Elisha, and the miraculous sustenance God provides to His people, reinforcing themes of faith, divine intervention, and covenantal blessing.
structure:
**Verses 1-7: The Widow's Oil Multiplied.** The chapter begins with a widow of a prophet's son seeking Elisha's help to save her children from slavery due to debt. Elisha instructs her to borrow vessels and pour out oil miraculously multiplied to pay her debts and provide for her family.

**Verses 8-17: The Shunammite Woman's Son.** A wealthy woman from Shunem provides hospitality to Elisha. In response, Elisha prophesies she will have a son despite her husband's old age. The promise is fulfilled, illustrating God's blessing through the prophet.

**Verses 18-37: The Resurrection of the Shunammite's Son.** The child later dies, and the mother seeks Elisha's help. After Gehazi's failed attempt, Elisha prays and performs a physical act of resurrection, restoring the boy to life, demonstrating God's power over death.

**Verses 38-41: The Poisonous Stew Purified.** During a famine, Elisha purifies a deadly stew for the sons of the prophets by adding meal, showing God's provision and protection.

**Verses 42-44: The Multiplication of Bread.** A man brings Elisha twenty barley loaves and ears of corn, which Elisha miraculously multiplies to feed a hundred men, affirming God's abundant provision through His prophet.

keyVerses.text: Then she came and told the man of God. And he said, Go, sell the oil, and pay thy debt, and live thou and thy children of the rest.
keyVerses.significance: This verse highlights God's provision through Elisha, showing that faith and obedience lead to deliverance from financial bondage and sustenance for the family.

keyVerses.text: And he said, About this season, according to the time of life, thou shalt embrace a son. And she said, Nay, my lord, thou man of God, do not lie unto thine handmaid.
keyVerses.significance: Elisha’s prophecy of a son to the barren Shunammite woman demonstrates God's power to bless and fulfill promises, reinforcing trust in divine providence.

keyVerses.text: Then he returned, and walked in the house to and fro ; and went up, and stretched himself upon him: and the child sneezed seven times, and the child opened his eyes.
keyVerses.significance: This verse records the miraculous resurrection of the Shunammite’s son, symbolizing God's authority over death and His compassion for His people.

keyVerses.text: But he said, Then bring meal. And he cast it into the pot; and he said, Pour out for the people, that they may eat. And there was no harm in the pot.
keyVerses.significance: Elisha’s purification of the poisonous stew illustrates God’s protection and care, assuring believers that He can make even dangerous situations safe.

keyVerses.text: So he set it before them, and they did eat, and left thereof, according to the word of the LORD.
keyVerses.significance: The miraculous multiplication of food confirms God's abundant provision and faithfulness to His promises, encouraging trust in His sustaining power.

characters.name: Elisha
characters.description: The prophet and central figure who performs miracles by God's power. He acts as God's instrument to provide, heal, and restore, demonstrating divine authority and compassion.

characters.name: The Widow
characters.description: A desperate woman whose husband, a prophet's son, has died leaving her in debt. She seeks Elisha’s help to save her sons from slavery, representing faith amidst hardship.

characters.name: The Shunammite Woman
characters.description: A wealthy and hospitable woman who recognizes Elisha's holiness. She provides him a room and is blessed with a son through Elisha’s prophecy, highlighting faith and God’s blessing.

characters.name: Gehazi
characters.description: Elisha’s servant who attempts to revive the Shunammite’s son with Elisha’s staff but fails, illustrating the necessity of the prophet’s direct intervention and God’s sovereign power.

characters.name: The Shunammite’s Son
characters.description: The miraculous child born to the Shunammite woman who later dies and is restored to life by Elisha, symbolizing God’s power over life and death.

themes.description: Throughout the chapter, God provides miraculously for physical needs—oil, food, and life—demonstrating His care for His people and reinforcing trust in His sustaining power.
The widow’s and Shunammite woman’s faith and obedience to Elisha’s instructions lead to miraculous outcomes, emphasizing the importance of trusting God’s word through His prophet.
Elisha’s role as God’s prophet is central; his words and actions bring life, healing, and provision, underscoring the divine authority vested in God’s messengers.
The raising of the Shunammite’s son prefigures God’s power over death, pointing forward to the ultimate resurrection hope found in Christ.
The chapter highlights God’s concern for widows, children, and the poor, showing His covenantal faithfulness to protect and provide for the marginalized.

historicalContext: This chapter is set in the 9th century BC during the divided monarchy period of Israel, specifically in the northern kingdom. Elisha, successor to Elijah, operates as a prophet in a politically unstable time marked by frequent conflicts and social challenges. The 'sons of the prophets' were groups of prophetic disciples living communally, often in rural or semi-rural settings, who sought spiritual renewal and guidance. Hospitality customs were highly valued, as seen in the Shunammite woman’s provision for Elisha. Debt slavery was a harsh reality for many, especially widows, making Elisha’s intervention critical for social justice and divine mercy. The geographic locations, such as Shunem and Gilgal, were significant centers in Israel’s tribal territories.

theologicalInterpretations.description: Reformed theology emphasizes God's sovereign grace in these miracles, viewing Elisha as a type of Christ who mediates God's provision and resurrection power. The chapter underscores God's covenant faithfulness and the necessity of faith and obedience.

Dispensationalists see Elisha’s miracles as part of God's progressive revelation and His dealings with Israel under the Old Testament covenant. These acts prefigure Christ’s ultimate miracles and the future restoration of Israel.

Early Church Fathers often interpreted the resurrection of the Shunammite’s son as a foreshadowing of Christ’s resurrection, highlighting the power of God over death and the hope of eternal life for believers.

crossReferences.connection: Jesus quotes Isaiah about bringing good news to the poor, mirroring Elisha’s ministry of provision and healing to the vulnerable.
Jesus declares Himself the resurrection and the life, paralleling Elisha’s raising of the Shunammite’s son as a sign of God’s power over death.
The Lord as shepherd provides and cares for His people, echoing the provision miracles in 2 Kings 4.
Jesus’ feeding of the five thousand with loaves and fishes reflects the miraculous multiplication of food in this chapter.
Faith is essential to please God, as demonstrated by the widow and Shunammite woman’s trust in Elisha’s word.

application: Trust God’s provision even in desperate circumstances, as the widow did by obeying Elisha’s instructions.
Show hospitality and care for God’s servants, knowing such faithfulness can lead to divine blessings.
Have faith in God’s promises, especially when they seem impossible, like the Shunammite woman’s conception.
Seek God’s help in times of loss and grief, trusting in His power to restore and heal.
Be attentive to God’s protection in daily life, relying on Him to safeguard against unseen dangers.
Practice generosity and share God’s blessings with others, trusting He will multiply what you give.
conclusion: 2 Kings Chapter 4 powerfully illustrates God’s compassionate provision and sovereign power through the prophet Elisha. The chapter’s miracles—multiplying oil and bread, granting a child, raising the dead, and purifying food—reveal a God who cares deeply for His people’s physical and spiritual needs. The faith and obedience of those involved serve as enduring examples for believers, encouraging trust in God’s promises and His ability to intervene miraculously. This chapter not only strengthens confidence in God’s providence but also foreshadows the greater works of Christ, inviting believers to rely wholly on God’s sustaining grace in every circumstance.

outline.heading: The Widow’s Oil Multiplied
outline.description: A widow in debt seeks Elisha’s help to save her sons from slavery. Elisha instructs her to gather vessels and pour out oil that miraculously multiplies, enabling her to pay debts and live.

outline.heading: The Shunammite Woman’s Hospitality and Promise of a Son
outline.description: A wealthy woman provides a room for Elisha. In gratitude, Elisha prophesies she will bear a son despite barrenness, and the promise is fulfilled.

outline.heading: The Resurrection of the Shunammite’s Son
outline.description: The Shunammite’s son dies unexpectedly. She seeks Elisha, who prays and miraculously restores the child to life, demonstrating God’s power over death.

outline.heading: The Poisonous Stew Purified
outline.description: During famine, Elisha purifies a deadly stew by adding meal, preventing death and providing safe nourishment for the sons of the prophets.

outline.heading: The Multiplication of Bread
outline.description: A man brings barley loaves and corn to Elisha, who miraculously multiplies the food to feed a hundred men, affirming God’s abundant provision.
